title: Earth's New Mini-Moon Is Staying for Christmas
summary: Earth has a new temporary neighbor, and it is staying for the holidays. Meet 2026 QQ8, a space rock only about 6 feet across. Scientists first spotted it in August 2026, after it slipped into orbit around Earth in April 2026. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center reported the discovery on October 29. QQ8 is called a mini-moon, or a temporary satellite, because Earth's gravity has caught it for a short visit. It will stay through December, then drift away in 2027. Scientists have worked out its path around the sun, which takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year. The rock swings close to Earth about once every ten years, but this time it came close enough for Earth's gravity to grab hold. At its nearest, QQ8 will pass about 353,000 miles from our planet. That is about 110,000 miles farther away than the average distance between Earth and the moon. There is no need to worry about a crash. Even if QQ8 headed straight for Earth, it would likely burn up completely in the atmosphere before reaching the ground. QQ8 is not the first mini-moon. Research last year suggested Earth could have as many as six mini-moons at any given time, and many of them may be fragments of our own moon. QQ8 is bigger than most. Modelling earlier this year suggested the average mini-moon is only about 75 centimeters across, or 30 inches, and the average stay lasts around nine months. Captured in April 2026, it should move on in January 2027. The same research suggested that a rock about 10 feet wide could stay caught for 10 to 20 years. For now, though, QQ8 is a short-term guest, a tiny traveler spending Christmas with Earth before heading back out into space.
why_it_matters: Mini-moons show how Earth's gravity can briefly capture passing space rocks, and studying them helps scientists understand near-Earth objects and where some of them may have come from.

background_read: A mini-moon is a small space rock that Earth's gravity catches for a short time, so it circles Earth like a tiny temporary moon instead of just flying past.
This happens when a rock traveling around the Sun comes close enough for Earth's pull to hold it for a while, even though it is not trapped forever.
Most of these visitors are very small and stay only for a short visit before Earth's gravity lets go and they drift back out into space.
Scientists study them because they can show how small rocks move near Earth and where some of them may have come from.
